ownership.short: Every value has exactly one owner. When the owner goes out of scope the value is dropped and its memory freed. No garbage collector, no manual free().
ownership.why: The single-owner rule is the root of Rust's memory safety, and the reason sharing, borrowing, and moving all have to be made explicit rather than assumed.

borrowing.short: Accessing a value through a reference (&T) without taking ownership. You can have many shared &T reads, or exactly one exclusive &mut T, but never both at once.
borrowing.why: Borrowing lets code use a value without moving it, and the one-writer-or-many-readers rule is what stops data races at compile time instead of in production.

move.short: Assigning or passing a non-Copy value transfers ownership; the source can no longer be used. `move` on a closure forces it to take ownership of what it captures.
move.why: A spawned task must own what it touches. `move` is how you hand ownership into a closure so it can outlive the function that created it.

lifetime.short: The span of code for which a reference stays valid. The compiler checks that no reference outlives the value it points at, sometimes with named annotations like 'a.
lifetime.why: Lifetimes are how Rust guarantees a reference can never dangle. Most are inferred; you only write them when the compiler can't tell which input a returned reference came from.

static-lifetime.short: A lifetime meaning "lives for the entire program." A value is 'static if it owns all its data (borrows nothing) or points at data baked into the binary.
static-lifetime.why: A task handed to a background executor must be 'static: it may outlive the function that spawned it, so it can't borrow anything on that function's stack.

send-sync.short: Marker traits the compiler infers automatically: Send means a value can be moved to another thread; Sync means it can be shared by reference across threads.
send-sync.why: They are what let the compiler reject cross-thread data races before the program runs. Arc is Send + Sync; Rc is neither, which is why spawn rejects it.

interior-mutability.short: A pattern where you mutate data through a shared (&T) reference, with a wrapper type (Cell, RefCell, Mutex) enforcing the borrow rules at runtime instead of compile time.
interior-mutability.why: Sometimes you genuinely need to mutate shared state; interior mutability moves the one-writer check to runtime so the compiler will allow it, and a Mutex is its thread-safe form.

reference-counting.short: Sharing ownership of one value among several owners by keeping a count of how many exist; the value is dropped when the last owner goes away. Rc for one thread, Arc across threads.
reference-counting.why: It's the escape hatch for when a single owner isn't enough. The count is the trade you make: cheap clones that share, at the cost of a runtime counter and no compile-time single-owner guarantee.

rc.short: A single-threaded reference-counted pointer. Cloning it bumps a non-atomic count and hands back another owner of the same value.
rc.why: Cheaper than Arc because the count isn't atomic, but that's exactly why it isn't Send: hand it to another thread and the compiler stops you. Reach for Arc when threads are involved.

arc.short: Atomically reference-counted shared pointer. Cloning it bumps a thread-safe refcount and hands back a second owner of the same value, not a copy.
arc.why: Lets two threads or tasks own one value at once. It is how a detached task can touch state the spawner still holds. Wrap it around a Mutex when the shared value also needs mutation.

weak.short: A non-owning reference to an Arc/Rc value. It doesn't keep the value alive; upgrade() returns None once the last strong owner is gone.
weak.why: Breaks reference cycles that would otherwise leak, and lets a map hold entries that clean themselves up: store Weak values and the map can drop the dead ones.

mutex.short: A lock guarding interior data so only one holder mutates at a time. tokio's async Mutex yields the task while waiting instead of blocking the whole thread.
mutex.why: Shared ownership alone still races on writes. The Mutex is what makes the shared mutation safe, and the compiler won't let you reach the data without taking the lock first.

async-await.short: async fn returns a future that does nothing until awaited; .await drives it and yields control back to the runtime while waiting, so one thread can juggle many tasks.
async-await.why: It's cooperative concurrency: awaiting a slow I/O call frees the thread to run other tasks instead of blocking, which is how a single process can supervise many servers at once.

tokio-spawn.short: Hands a future to the tokio runtime to run concurrently, returning a JoinHandle. The task may run on any worker thread and may outlive the caller, so it must be 'static and Send.
tokio-spawn.why: The go-to way to run work in the background. Its 'static + Send bounds are exactly why detached tasks reach for Arc<Mutex<T>> instead of borrowing the caller's state.

timeout.short: Wraps a future with a deadline; it resolves to Err once the duration elapses, cancelling the inner future.
timeout.why: Bounds how long async work may take so a hung boot or a wedged health check turns into a clean, reportable failure instead of a task that waits forever.

option.short: An enum that is either Some(value) or None. Rust has no null; absence is a value you must handle, checked by the compiler.
option.why: "Might be missing" becomes a case the type forces you to consider, so you can't accidentally use a value that isn't there. Serde fills a missing field with None for you.

result.short: An enum that is either Ok(value) or Err(error). Rust has no exceptions; a fallible operation returns its error as a value you must handle.
result.why: Failure is in the type signature, so you can't ignore it by accident. How you handle the Err (surface it, default it, propagate it) becomes a deliberate choice at each call site.

question-mark.short: On a Result or Option, ? unwraps the Ok/Some value or early-returns the Err/None from the enclosing function. It replaces a match that would just propagate the error.
question-mark.why: Turns manual error-forwarding into one character, keeping the happy path readable while still handling every failure explicitly.

combinators.short: Methods on Option/Result that transform them without a match: map, and_then, ok, unwrap_or, unwrap_or_else, and friends. Each takes a closure or a default.
combinators.why: They express "do this if present, else that" as a chain instead of a branch. The distinction matters: unwrap_or throws the error away, unwrap_or_else hands it to you first.

match.short: match compares a value against patterns and must cover every case; if let is the shorthand for when you only care about one pattern and ignore the rest.
match.why: Exhaustive matching means adding a new enum variant makes the compiler point you at every place that must handle it, so "forgot a case" becomes a build error.

closure.short: An anonymous function written with |args| body that can capture variables from its surrounding scope, by reference or (with move) by value.
closure.why: Closures are how you pass behavior around: a combinator's transform, a task's body, a Drop guard's cleanup. What they capture, and whether they move it, decides their lifetime.

iterator.short: A lazy sequence: .iter() and adapters like .map() build a pipeline that does no work until something drives it. Nothing is computed until you consume it.
iterator.why: Laziness means you can chain transforms cheaply and only pay for what you actually take. The pipeline stays declarative; collect (or a for loop) is what makes it run.

collect.short: Consumes an iterator and gathers its items into a collection (Vec, HashMap, String, ...). It's the driver that finally runs a lazy iterator pipeline.
collect.why: Turns one collection into another in a single expression, with the target type telling collect what to build. It's where a map/filter chain stops being lazy and produces a value.

trait.short: A named set of methods a type can implement, like an interface. Code can then require "any type that implements this trait" rather than one concrete type.
trait.why: Traits are Rust's main tool for shared behavior and abstraction, and implementing a library's trait is how you plug your own type into that library's machinery.

generics.short: Writing code over a type parameter (like T or S) instead of a concrete type, so one function or struct works for many types.
generics.why: Write the logic once and let the compiler specialize it per type. Combined with trait bounds, generics give you abstraction with no runtime cost.

trait-bound.short: A constraint on a generic type, written like T: Display, saying "T must implement this trait." It's what lets generic code actually call methods on T.
trait-bound.why: The bound is the contract: it tells the compiler which methods are available on the type parameter, and tells callers which types they're allowed to pass.

static-dispatch.short: Resolving which concrete method to call at compile time. Generic code is monomorphized into a specialized copy per type, so calls are direct with no runtime lookup.
static-dispatch.why: It's abstraction for free: the generic loop over a stream type compiles down to the same machine code you'd have written by hand for each concrete type.

dynamic-dispatch.short: Resolving the method at runtime through a trait object (dyn Trait), which carries a pointer to the right implementation. One code path handles many types.
dynamic-dispatch.why: Trades a tiny runtime indirection for flexibility: you can store different implementing types together or choose one at runtime, which generics can't do.

monomorphization.short: The compiler's process of turning generic code into concrete code by stamping out a specialized copy for each type it's used with.
monomorphization.why: It's why generics have zero runtime overhead: by the time the program runs, each generic use is just ordinary type-specific code. The cost is paid in compile time and binary size.

drop.short: The Drop trait runs cleanup code automatically when a value goes out of scope. Tie a resource's release to a value's lifetime and you can't forget to free it.
drop.why: Files close, locks release, and guards fire without a manual step. The catch: a signal-killed process skips destructors, so external cleanup can't rely on Drop alone.

newtype.short: Wrapping a value in a single-field struct to give it a distinct type, so a validated or domain-specific value can't be confused with a plain one.
newtype.why: The wrapper is where you enforce an invariant once (a HeaderValue is a validated byte-string, not any String), and the type system carries that guarantee everywhere after.

derive-macro.short: A #[derive(...)] attribute that generates a trait implementation for your type at compile time, so you don't hand-write boilerplate impls.
derive-macro.why: One line gives you the code for common traits (Debug, Clone, and serde's Serialize/Deserialize). You only hand-write the impl when the derived shape isn't exactly what you need.

serde.short: serde's two traits for converting Rust values to and from formats like JSON or TOML. Usually derived; #[serde(...)] attributes tune field names, defaults, and shape.
serde.why: Deriving them on a dedicated DTO type pins your public wire format to a Rust type, so the contract lives in code and the compiler keeps the two in sync.

unsafe-ffi.short: unsafe marks code where you, not the compiler, uphold the safety rules, typically to call across a foreign function interface (FFI) into C or a system library.
unsafe-ffi.why: It's the escape hatch for things the borrow checker can't verify, like calling into the OS keychain. The unsafe block is a deliberate, auditable boundary, not a free-for-all.

instant.short: Instant is a monotonic clock for measuring elapsed time; SystemTime is the wall clock that can jump backward when the OS adjusts it.
instant.why: For deadlines and timeouts you want Instant, because it never goes backward. Reach for SystemTime only when you need an actual calendar time.

vec.short: A growable, heap-allocated array of T. It owns its elements and frees them when it's dropped.
vec.why: The default owned collection. Building one with the vec![] macro or by collecting an iterator is the everyday way to hold a variable number of values.

hashmap.short: A hash-table mapping owned keys to owned values, with average O(1) insert and lookup.
hashmap.why: The standard key-value store. It owns what you put in it, and methods like retain let you edit it in place without rebuilding it.

hashmap-retain.short: Keeps only the entries for which a closure returns true, removing the rest in one in-place pass over the map.
hashmap-retain.why: The idiomatic way to garbage-collect a map (for example, dropping entries whose Weak value has expired) without allocating a new one or iterating twice.

str-vs-string.short: String is an owned, growable UTF-8 buffer; &str is a borrowed view into one (or into a string literal). String owns, &str borrows.
str-vs-string.why: The distinction is ownership again: take &str in function arguments to borrow without allocating, and return String when the caller needs to own the result.

split-once.short: Cuts a string at the first occurrence of a delimiter into two borrowed &str slices, returning Option so "delimiter not found" is a None case, not a panic.
split-once.why: Exactly right for parsing key=value or label.name: you get both halves as borrows of the original, and the Option makes the missing-delimiter case something you handle, not a bug.

format-macro.short: Builds a new String from a template, filling {} placeholders with values. {name} captures a variable of that name directly from scope.
format-macro.why: The everyday way to assemble strings. Its inline-capture form keeps templated text readable, and it's how derived data like a URL or an env value gets composed.

build-rs.short: A build script: Rust code the compiler runs before compiling your crate. Printing cargo:rustc-env=KEY=VALUE injects a value the crate can read at compile time.
build-rs.why: It's how compile-time facts (a git SHA, a build timestamp) get baked into the binary, so the program can report exactly which build it is without any runtime lookup.

env-macro.short: Compile-time macros that read an environment variable and bake it into the binary as a &'static str. env! fails the build if it's unset; option_env! yields an Option instead.
env-macro.why: Paired with build.rs, they turn build-time environment values into constants compiled into the program, so there's nothing to read or fail at runtime.

include-str.short: A macro that reads a file at compile time and embeds its contents into the binary as a &'static str.
include-str.why: Bakes a whole document (a template, a help text) into the executable, so it ships as one self-contained file with nothing to load from disk at runtime.

command.short: The builder for spawning a child process: chain .env(), .arg(), .stdout() to configure it, then .spawn(). It inherits the parent's environment by default.
command.why: A textbook builder pattern, and the surface where a supervisor injects a child's port and environment before starting it, one .env() layer at a time.
